judge_assessment.explanation: I recomputed all twelve stories from the printed numbers and every one matches the judge's list and verify.json: 45+10+20 = 75 min; 95-(40+25) = 30 min; 20-(8.75+3.50) = $7.75; 3x25 + 4x10 - 55 = 60 cents; 250+180+400 = 830 g; 2000-2x350 = 1300 mL; 5x25+40 = 165 min; 50-4x6 = $26; 3000-2x450 = 2100 g; 5000-(1200+1500) = 2300 mL; 35x2x5 = 350 min; 50-6x(3+2x2) = $8. The judge's claim that the key retains units through both steps holds — every solution states the intermediate quantity with its unit ('430 g', '2000 mL', '$12.25') before the boxed answer. I also checked the two things the judge did not state but which the contract requires. Every problem is genuinely two-step (no single-operation item slipped in), and every printed answer slot has exactly one verify entry: there are no explanation stems, no drawing tasks and no multi-part items on this sheet, so neither of the run's two dominant systemic defects applies here. That is unusual in this batch and it is why I agree with 32/32 without qualification on the artifacts. The only inaccuracy I found is in the delivery text rather than in the material: final_response.md claims 'Every problem has a printed answer line with the unit already on it (minutes, cents, g, mL)', while problems 3, 8 and 12 — the dollars problems — carry bare answer lines.

strengths_to_preserve: Three problems force a unit conversion INSIDE the story rather than as a separate exercise: problem 6 pours 350 mL glasses from a 2 L jug, problem 9 removes 450 g books from a 3 kg box, problem 10 draws 1200 and 1500 mL from a 5 L cooler. The conversion is the step children skip, and the sheet makes it unskippable while leaving the arithmetic grade-appropriate.

The 'wrong conversion factor' trap on problem 6 is declared as expr 'j*100 - n*g' — using 100 mL in a litre instead of 1000 — so the misconception is machine-proved to give a different (negative) result, and the key can name it instead of marking a number wrong.

Problem 11's key shows both valid orders of the two steps ('2 x 5 = 10 rides, then 10 x 35 = 350' and 'or 2 x 35 = 70 minutes a day, then 5 x 70 = 350'), which is the right treatment for a problem whose whole point is that the child chooses the grouping.

The interleave and the closing synthesis both do what the mode asks: the first four problems block by kind as the warm-up, then the four kinds rotate (mass, volume, time, money, mass, volume, time, money), and problem 12 is the only item combining a per-group cost, a repeated group, and change from a starting amount.

Nine of the twelve answers carry a declared answer_unit bound in both directions — the sheet prints 'Answer: ____ minutes / cents / g / mL' and the key boxes '75 minutes', '60 cents', '830 g', '1300 mL' — so a millilitre problem cannot be answered in litres without failing a gate.

root_causes.description: final_response.md states a universal claim about the artifacts that three of the twelve problems contradict. The material is right — tests/_units.py documents that prefix currency symbols are out of scope for the unit gates and instructs authors to 'write "in dollars" in the problem stem instead of declaring a currency answer_unit', which is exactly what problems 3, 8 and 12 do — so this is a reporting defect, not a worksheet defect. But the delivery text is what a parent reads to know what they are holding, and an unqualified 'every problem' that is false for a quarter of the sheet erodes the value of every other claim in the same document.
evidence: final_response.md: 'Every problem has a printed answer line with the unit already on it (minutes, cents, g, mL), so the answer is written where a grader will look and in the unit the question asked for.'
worksheet.pdf problems 3, 8 and 12 print 'Answer: ________' with no unit; the stems carry 'Give your answer in dollars' instead.
verify.json declares answer_unit for ids 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11 only — nine of twelve.
final_response.md also generalises 'The units are verified too, in both directions', which is true of those nine and vacuous for the other three.

tests/_units.py docstring: 'PREFIX currency symbols ($5, \$) are out of scope — the dollar sign doubles as the math delimiter and cannot be token-matched safely. Write "in dollars" in the problem stem instead of declaring a currency answer_unit.'

improvements.title: Quantify coverage claims in the final response instead of asserting universals the artifacts do not support
improvements.proposed_change: Add a short rule to SKILL.md's delivery section: coverage sentences in final_response.md must be counted, not asserted — 'nine of the twelve answer lines carry a printed unit; the three money answers say "in dollars" in the stem instead, because the unit gates cannot token-match a leading dollar sign' rather than 'every problem has a printed answer line with the unit already on it'. The same rule covers the more damaging variant seen elsewhere in this batch, where 'nothing is flagged for manual review' is asserted on sheets that ask a child to write an explanation. The numbers are already available: the driver knows how many ids declare answer_unit and how many entries are type manual, so the response can quote the counts it is given rather than generalising from a majority.
improvements.regression_test: Extend tests/test_curriculum_eval_suite.py with a delivery-claim check over a fixture case: given a verify.json where 9 of 12 ids declare answer_unit and a final_response.md containing the phrase 'every problem has a printed answer line with the unit', assert the check exits 1; rewrite the sentence to name the count ('nine of the twelve') and assert exit 0. The check should be a narrow lexical rule over universal quantifiers adjacent to coverage nouns (unit, verified, manual review), not a general claim verifier.
improvements.expected_impact: A parent or teacher can trust the summary as an inventory rather than as marketing. It also gives the author system a single discipline that covers both this small overstatement and the 'nothing is flagged for manual review' claims that are actively wrong on four other cases in this batch.
improvements.risk: Over-literal enforcement would make the delivery text stilted, and a lexical quantifier check will misfire on legitimate universals ('every problem is two-step' is true here and should pass). Keep the rule to coverage nouns, keep it advisory in SKILL.md with the mechanical check narrow, and accept that the main remedy is the instruction rather than the gate.

case_summary: A clean case and the only one in this batch where neither dominant systemic defect appears. All twelve two-step answers recompute correctly, including the three that require a unit conversion inside the story (2 L against 350 mL glasses, 3 kg against 450 g books, 5 L against two millilitre draws) and the closing synthesis (six groups at $3 + 2x$2, change from $50, giving $8). Every problem has exactly one printed answer slot and exactly one verify entry; there are no explanation stems, no drawing tasks and no multi-part items, so nothing is silently unchecked, and nine of the twelve answers carry an answer_unit bound in both directions between the sheet's answer line and the key's boxed answer. The traps are well chosen — the '100 mL in a litre' error, taking out one book instead of two, counting only the outbound bus ride — and each is machine-proved to land on a different number. My one finding is in the delivery text, not the material: final_response.md claims every problem's answer line carries its unit, when the three dollars problems deliberately carry none, because tests/_units.py documents that a leading dollar sign cannot be token-matched and instructs authors to put 'in dollars' in the stem — which is what the sheet correctly does. The artifact is right and the sentence describing it is wrong.
